questions.worked_solution:
Given two $n\times n$ matrices $M$ and $N,$ we have

$$
det(MN)=det(M)\cdot det(N).
$$

In our case, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}det(C) & =det[\begin{aligned}2 & 6 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]\cdot det[\begin{aligned}6\sqrt{3} & 2 \\ 5 & 2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =(8-18)\cdot (36-10) \\  & =(-10)\cdot 26 \\  & =-260.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Determinant of the Inverse of a Matrix
questions.worked_solution:
Given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have

$$
det({A}^{-1})=\frac{1}{det(A)}.
$$

First, we find $det(A):$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =det[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =12+3 \\  & =15\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
det({A}^{-1})=\frac{1}{det(A)}=\frac{1}{15}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Determinant of the Inverse of a Matrix
questions.worked_solution:
Given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have

$$
|{A}^{-1}|=\frac{1}{|A|}.
$$

First, we find $|A|$ using a Laplace expansion across the $3$rd row:

$$
\begin{aligned}|A| & =|\begin{aligned}-7 & 3 & 5 \\ 6 & -4 & 1 \\ -2 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2\cdot (-1)^{3+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-2)\cdot (3+20) \\  & =-46\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
|{A}^{-1}|=\frac{1}{|A|}=-\frac{1}{46}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Determinant Using the Linearity of the Determinant
questions.problem:
Given that 
$|\begin{aligned}a+2 & -2 & 2 \\ b+3 & 4 & 2 \\ c & 0 & 1\end{aligned}|=5,$
find 
$|\begin{aligned}a+1 & -2 & 2 \\ b & 4 & 2 \\ c & 0 & 1\end{aligned}|.$
questions.worked_solution:
We "factor out" the given determinant from the determinant we would like to find:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}a+1 & -2 & 2 \\ b & 4 & 2 \\ c & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}(a+2)-1 & -2 & 2 \\ (b+3)-3 & 4 & 2 \\ c+0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

  

Now, using the linearity property of determinants and expanding the second determinant across the $3$rd row, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}(a+2)-1 & -2 & 2 \\ (b+3)-3 & 4 & 2 \\ c+0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| & ={{|\begin{aligned}(a+2) & -2 & 2 \\ (b+3) & 4 & 2 \\ c & 0 & 1\end{aligned}|}_{⏟}}_{5}+|\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 2 \\ -3 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =5+1\cdot (-1)^{3+3}|\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =5+(-10) \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Determinant Using the Linearity of the Determinant
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the $1$st row of our determinant is almost equal to the $3$rd row. So, we can rewrite the given determinant, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}160 & 184 & 76 \\ 3 & 4 & -8 \\ 160 & 184 & 78\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}160 & 184 & 76 \\ 3 & 4 & -8 \\ 160+0 & 184+0 & 76+2\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Next, using the linearity property of determinants, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}160 & 184 & 76 \\ 3 & 4 & -8 \\ 160+0 & 184+0 & 76+2\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}160 & 184 & 76 \\ 3 & 4 & -8 \\ 160 & 184 & 76\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}160 & 184 & 76 \\ 3 & 4 & -8 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

The first determinant must be zero since it has two identical rows, while the second determinant can be expanded across the $3$rd row, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}160 & 184 & 76 \\ 3 & 4 & -8 \\ 160 & 184 & 76\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}160 & 184 & 76 \\ 3 & 4 & -8 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0+2(-1)^{3+3}|\begin{aligned}160 & 184 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot (160\cdot 4-184\cdot 3) \\  & =2\cdot 88 \\  & =176\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that 
$|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ a & b+2\end{aligned}|=8$,
find 
$|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ a+3 & b\end{aligned}|.$
questions.worked_solution:
We "factor out" the given determinant from the determinant we would like to find:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ a+3 & b\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ a+3 & (b+2)-2\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the linearity property of determinants, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ a+3 & (b+2)-2\end{aligned}| & ={{|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ a & b+2\end{aligned}|}_{⏟}}_{8}+|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =8+(-6+6) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that 
$|\begin{aligned}a & b & c \\ 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}|=4,$
find 
$|\begin{aligned}a+1 & b & c \\ 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}|.$
questions.worked_solution:
We "factor out" the given determinant from the determinant we would like to find:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}a+1 & b & c \\ 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}a+1 & b+0 & c+0 \\ 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the linearity property of determinants and expanding the second determinant across the $1$st row, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}a+1 & b+0 & c+0 \\ 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & ={{|\begin{aligned}a & b & c \\ 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}|}_{⏟}}_{4}+|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =4+1(-1)^{1+1}|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =4+1 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Determinant of the Inverse of a Matrix
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have

$$
|A^{-1}| = \dfrac{1}{|A|}.
$$

First, we find $|A|$ using a Laplace expansion across the $3$rd row:

$$
\begin{aligned}|A| & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 14 & -1 \\ 7 & -6 & -6 \\ 0 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3(-1)^{3+2}|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 7 & -6\end{aligned}| \\  & =3\cdot (-12+7) \\  & =-15\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\det(A^{-1}) =  \dfrac{1}{|A|} = -\dfrac{1}{15}.
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We "factor out" the given determinant from the determinant we would like to find:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}a & b & c+1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}a+0 & b+0 & c+1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the linearity property of determinants and expanding the second determinant across the $1$st row, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}a+0 & b+0 & c+1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| & ={{|\begin{aligned}a & b & c \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}|}_{⏟}}_{-10}+|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-10+1(-1)^{1+3}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-10-1 \\  & =-11.\end{aligned}
$$
